Spectral Analysis with the DFT and Block Convolution (L06, second half)

Why this matters in the exam: This is the last part of Lecture 6: “Linear filtering based on the DFT” (slides 23–28) and “Frequency analysis using the DFT” (slides 29–32). L05–L10 have never been tested. Sample Test 1 (20 marks, 50 min) stops at Week 4, so there is no past-paper evidence of marks. The only tutorial questions on this half are T5 Q4 (DFT deconvolution, which is really a wrap-around problem) and T5 Q5 (choosing , and ). Expect a short calculation of the T5 Q5 type (about 3–4 marks), and possibly a hand overlap-add or overlap-save on short sequences, or a “why use a Hanning window” explanation (2–5 marks).

Pack D5 covers the DFT definition, its properties and circular convolution. This pack assumes you can do a short circular convolution.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The DFT as a spectrum analyser (slide 29)

The lecture’s three steps for analysing an analogue signal:

  1. Anti-aliasing lowpass filter.
  2. Sample at , where is the highest signal frequency.
  3. Keep samples, so the record length is . This limits the frequency resolution (the ability to separate two components) to .

You then take an -point DFT (, zero-padded if ).

Quantity Formula What it is Trap
Sampling interval time between samples —
Record length how long you actually observed the signal Uses (real samples), not
Frequency resolution smallest separation you can resolve Zero-padding does not change it
Bin spacing gap between DFT sample frequencies Gets finer with zero-padding, but that is only interpolation
Bin frequency , analogue frequency of bin Valid for ; bin is the mirror image

When there is no zero-padding (), the resolution and the bin spacing are the same number, , and . This is the case in T5 Q5, whose solution uses “Resolution ” and .

Note on slide 30. The slide writes . Read this as with , which gives . That is the same as the DFT sampling points from slide 5.

1.2 Choosing , and

You are given a bandwidth and a required resolution (and often “” because of the FFT).

The trap is rounding. always rounds up, because a larger gives a finer resolution. After rounding, the actual resolution is better than required. Use the minimum unless told otherwise, because a higher needs a larger for the same resolution.

1.3 Zero-padding (slides 9–10)

Zero-padding samples to length samples the same DTFT at more points ( apart instead of ).

  • It gives a smoother picture and a better estimate of where a peak is. This is interpolation.
  • It adds no new information about the signal. Two tones closer than stay merged, whatever is.

Slide 9 says zero-padding gives “better resolution for sampled DTFT”. That means a finer frequency grid. It does not mean better ability to separate tones. In an exam, keep the two words apart: write “bin spacing” for and “resolution” for .

1.4 Windowing and leakage (slides 30–32)

Keeping samples is the same as multiplying by a rectangular window:

Multiplication in time is convolution in frequency, so . (Slide 30 omits the , which is just a scale factor; the L06 multiplication property, slide 20, has it.) Each spectral line of is replaced by a copy of . is a sinc-like function with a main lobe and side lobes. Energy smeared out of the true frequency is called leakage (slide 32).

Bin-aligned or not. A sinusoid at sits at the non-integer bin .

  • If is an integer and (a whole number of cycles in the record), every other DFT sample falls on a zero of . You see one clean line, with height for .
  • If is not an integer, the DFT samples land on the side lobes. Every bin gets some energy. This is leakage, and the peak is also lower (called “scalloping”).

The Hanning window (slide 32):

It tapers both ends of the record to zero, so the record has no sudden jumps at its edges.

Rectangular Hanning
Main lobe (null to null) (2 bins when ) about (about 4 bins)
Highest side lobe dB dB
Side-lobe fall-off slow fast
Peak of an aligned tone about (the window’s average is about 0.5)
Use when tones are close and similar in size a weak tone sits near a strong one, or a tone is not bin-aligned

(Side-lobe and main-lobe values computed numerically for ; they are the standard figures.)

The trade-off in one line: Hanning lowers the side lobes (less leakage) but doubles the main-lobe width (worse resolution). With Hanning you need about twice the record length to separate the same two tones.

This is Figure 1’s tone at . Slide to 8.0 and the leakage vanishes; set it back to 8.5 and switch between rectangular and Hann to see the side lobes drop and the main lobe widen. Turn on zero-padding and note that the peaks do not get any narrower.

1.5 Block convolution (slides 25–27)

Slide 24: when . For a long input, split it into blocks of new samples () and use point DFTs. Zero-pad from to samples once. Then is computed once and reused for every block.

Overlap-add (slide 27) Overlap-save (slide 26)
Input block new samples followed by zeros (length ) the last samples of the previous block followed by new samples (length ). The first block starts with zeros
Is the circular result correct? Yes, all outputs equal the linear convolution of the block The first outputs are wrong (time-aliased); the last are correct
Combine Overlap each block’s outputs at a shift of and add the overlapping samples Discard the first outputs of each block; place the remaining side by side
Blocks needed for all outputs

Why overlap-save works. In an -point circular convolution of a length- block with a length- filter, the linear result is long. Its last samples wrap round onto outputs . So exactly the first outputs are corrupted. The same thing happens in T5 Q4 with : only is wrong.

Hand shortcut (no DFTs needed). In an exam you do the circular convolutions by hand, not with DFTs:

  • Overlap-add: the block (length ) (length ) is exactly long. So the circular convolution is the ordinary linear convolution. Just convolve.
  • Overlap-save: linearly convolve the length- block with (result long). Then add the last samples onto the first . That gives the -point circular result (this is time aliasing, as in D5).

Playbook C: zero-padding and resolution

Playbook D: windowing

  1. Check bin alignment ( an integer?). If it is aligned and you use a rectangular window, there is no leakage.
  2. If not aligned, a rectangular window gives side lobes at dB falling only slowly (about dB 2 bins away, dB 6 bins away).
  3. If a weak component must be seen near a strong one, use Hanning. Its side lobes are dB and fall fast.
  4. Pay for it in main-lobe width (about 4 bins null to null), so lengthen the record if the tones are close.
  5. Always state the trade-off in your answer: “lower side lobes, wider main lobe”.

  1. Write (filter length) and (new samples per block). . If is given, .

  4. OLS: for each block, find the -point circular convolution with (linear convolution, then fold the last samples onto the front). Discard the first outputs. Keep .

  • With the rectangular window, the peak drops from 32 to about 20.8 (about dB). Every bin is non-zero: this is leakage. ( because the mirror tone at leaks too.)
  • With Hanning, the peak is lower in absolute terms, because the window averages about 0.5 (an aligned tone would give about 15.75, not 32). But leakage at bin 12 (3.5 bins from the tone) is about 24 dB lower than with the rectangular window, and it keeps falling fast.

Answer: the aligned tone gives one line of height 32 at (and ). The off-bin tone spreads into every bin. Hanning confines it to about bins 7–10 at the cost of a wider peak.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using instead of for resolution after zero-padding. Resolution is . is only the bin spacing.
  • Claiming zero-padding improves resolution. It interpolates the same DTFT. Slide 9’s “better resolution” means a finer grid.
  • Rounding down, or forgetting to round to a power of 2 when the question says (T5 Q5: 120 becomes 128, not 64).
  • Forgetting the mirror bin. A real cosine at also appears at . Bin is a negative frequency, not a frequency above .
  • Calling Hanning “better” without the cost. It lowers side lobes but widens the main lobe (about 2×). Full marks need both halves.
  • Overlap-save: forgetting the leading zeros in the first block, or carrying over samples instead of .
  • Overlap-save: discarding the last outputs instead of the first. The wrap-around corrupts the start of each block.
  • Overlap-add: forgetting to add the overlap, or overlapping by instead of . Block starts at .

N5. [5 marks] A signal sampled at kHz contains a strong tone at 1010 Hz (amplitude 1) and a weak tone at 1050 Hz (amplitude 0.01, i.e.  dB). You are told that the worst-case leakage of a tone into a bin or more bins away is:

(bins) 2 3 4 5 6
Rectangular dB dB dB dB dB
Hanning dB dB dB dB dB
  1. Which window must be used, and why? [2]
  2. Find the minimum power-of-2 record length (with ) so that the weak tone is at least 5 bins from the strong one. Give . [2]
  3. What would you see with a rectangular window and the same ? [1]
Solution

  1. Hanning. The weak tone is 40 dB down. The rectangular window’s leakage never gets below about dB within 6 bins, so it would bury the weak tone. The strong tone is not bin-aligned in general, so you cannot rely on zero leakage. Hanning’s side lobes drop below dB by 5 bins. The price is a wider main lobe, which is why (b) asks for 5 bins of separation.

  2. Separation 40 Hz , so . Round up: , 0.128 s (bin spacing 7.81 Hz, so the tones are 5.12 bins apart).

  3. Rectangular, : the leakage from 1010 Hz at the weak tone’s bins is about dB, which is above the weak tone ( dB). No separate peak is visible.

Numerical check (Python, ): with Hanning, the weak tone’s bin is at dB and its neighbours are at and dB, so there is a clear local peak. With rectangular, the same bin is at dB with neighbours at and dB, so there is no peak. With Hanning and (2.56 bins apart), there is no peak either.

  2. Hz, so . Round up to . 42.7 ms. Resolution 23.4 Hz Hz.

  3. Bin spacing 23.4375 Hz. 64 (bin-aligned, so no leakage on its own). 65.28 (not aligned, so it leaks into all bins, with its peak near ). The mirror images are at and . Caveat: Hz is the course’s rule, and by that rule the tones count as resolved. On a real plot, though, the two tones sit only 1.28 bins apart, so you may not see a clear dip between two peaks. In practice you want a margin above .

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

SPECTRAL ANALYSIS (L06 s29-32)
 Fs >= 2B        Ts = 1/Fs        T0 = L*Ts = L/Fs   (L = real samples)
 Resolution  = 1/T0 = Fs/L        Bin spacing = Fs/N   (same if no zero-pad)
 Bin freq    F_k = k*Fs/N,  w_k = 2*pi*k/N;  k > N/2  ->  -(N-k)*Fs/N
 Real tone F0 -> bins k0 = F0*N/Fs and N-k0; non-integer k0 => leakage
 Design: Fs = 2B; N >= Fs/dF, round UP to 2^m; T0 = N/Fs; quote Fs/N
 Zero-padding: finer grid (interpolation) only, NO new resolution
 Aligned A*cos, rect, N = L: |X(k0)| = A*N/2, all other bins 0
 Hanning: w(n) = 0.5(1 - cos(2*pi*n/(L-1))), 0 <= n < L
   rect : main lobe 2 bins (4pi/L), sidelobe -13 dB
   hann : main lobe ~4 bins (8pi/L), sidelobe -31 dB, gain ~0.5
   => less leakage, worse resolution (budget ~2x the record length)

BLOCK CONVOLUTION (L06 s25-27)   N = L + M - 1, h zero-padded to N once
 OLA: blocks of L + (M-1) zeros; block*h = linear (exactly N long);
      place block i at n = iL; ADD the M-1 overlapping samples
 OLS: block = last M-1 of previous + L new (first block: M-1 zeros);
      circular = linear conv, then fold the last M-1 onto the first M-1;
      DISCARD the first M-1 outputs, keep L
 Blocks: OLA ceil(Lx/L);  OLS ceil((Lx+M-1)/L);  total output Lx+M-1
 T5 Q4 is OLS with M=2: n=0 wrong; fix with +0.5*y(63)
